# Vibration After Engine Mount Change

Replacing engine mounts on a Renault Grand Scenic II (2005, 1.6 16v) is often a cure-all for excessive drivetrain vibration, but it can also be a diagnostic trap if the new hardware isn't matched to the underlying mechanical reality. You have already executed a comprehensive teardown: shocks, wishbone arms, track rod ends, anti-roll bars, springs, clutch system, head gasket set, timing belt, and every filter. The fact that the vibration persists after installing fresh engine, gearbox, and exhaust mounts suggests we are looking at a dynamic imbalance or a residual mechanical fault rather than simple rubber degradation.

The symptom you describedâvibrating violently when pumping the brake pedal while stationary, then dying downâis highly specific. This behavior points to an issue with the drivetrain's ability to dampen torque fluctuations or a misalignment that only manifests under load changes. When you pump the brakes, you are momentarily locking the wheels, which can cause the engine RPM to drop rapidly if the clutch is engaged, or create a sudden load shift on the transmission. If the vibration stops after four or five seconds, it implies the system is finding a new equilibrium or that a specific component is resonating at idle but settling once the engine speed stabilizes slightly.

The fact that the vibration worsens in 5th gear compared to 4th at 50 mph is a critical data point. In a manual transmission vehicle like the Grand Scenic II, shifting from 4th to 5th lowers the engine RPM for a given road speed. This change alters the firing order frequency relative to the drivetrain's natural resonant frequency. If you feel significantly more aggression in the steering wheel and gas pedal in 5th gear, it strongly suggests an imbalance in the rotating assembly (crankshaft, flywheel, or harmonic balancer) that becomes audible and tactile when the engine spins at a specific lower RPM range. It is also possible that the new mounts are installed with incorrect torque specifications or orientation, causing the engine to sit slightly off-center, which amplifies any existing imbalance.

Another common oversight after mount replacement is the condition of the transmission input shaft splines or the flywheel surface. If the old clutch job did not include resurfacing the flywheel to a perfect flatness or replacing a damaged pressure plate, the new clutch disc may be engaging unevenly. This can cause high-frequency vibrations that feel like engine shake but originate from the torque converter (in automatics) or the release bearing (in manuals). Given that you mentioned the old mount was so worn the engine could move by hand, it is possible that the engine was slightly rotated during removal and installation, altering the alignment of the powertrain. Even a few millimeters of offset can cause excessive play in the new mounts under load.

To isolate this further without tearing the car down again, you should inspect the harmonic balancer (crankshaft damper). Many older 1.6 Renault engines suffer from internal cracks or separation in the rubber ring of this component. When the engine vibrates at certain RPMs, this crack can open and close, creating a rhythmic thrum that travels through the chassis and into the steering wheel. This mimics mount failure but is actually an imbalance issue.

If the mounts are confirmed new and correctly torqued, and the harmonic balancer is sound, the diagnosis likely lies in a bent driveshaft or a universal joint (U-joint) that is binding at specific angles. The vibration worsening in 5th gear could also indicate a mismatch in final drive ratio if the transmission was rebuilt without matching the correct gears, though this is less common than mechanical imbalance.

For a definitive resolution, consider having a shop perform a laser alignment check on the engine and gearbox while the car is jacked up but supported by stands. This ensures the new mounts are seated perfectly parallel to the chassis rails. If that yields no results, the harmonic balancer must be removed and inspected for internal separation. Ignoring this step risks repeating the repair cycle with fresh money spent on components that cannot fix a rotating assembly imbalance.
